item.title: Claude Opus 5.5 generated a six-hour interactive visualization of Italo Calvino's Invisible Cities from a single prompt [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A developer tested Claude Opus 5.5's design capabilities by giving it one prompt and six hours to create an interactive three.js visualization of all 55 cities from Italo Calvino's Invisible Cities. The AI completed the task in about 1 hour 25 minutes using six parallel subagents, producing a detailed and polished result that impressed the creator despite not using the full allotted time. The experiment compared Claude Opus 5.5's output with earlier models like GPT-6 Astra, which took longer and cost less but produced noisier designs. The project highlights advances in AI-assisted design for interactive media and raises questions about the evolving role of human creators in such workflows.

item.title: StepFun releases Step 5 Preview, a 1M-context Mixture of Experts model, on OpenRouter [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: StepFun has launched Step 5 Preview, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model capable of handling a 1 million token context window, on the OpenRouter platform. This release highlights advancements in large-context language models and their accessibility through open platforms. The model's availability on OpenRouter allows developers and researchers to experiment with extended context capabilities in AI applications.

item.title: Trump says calling AI 'the enemy' is wrong, noting the White House uses AI technology [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Former President Donald Trump stated that labeling artificial intelligence as 'the enemy' is incorrect, highlighting that the White House itself employs AI technology. His remarks reflect contrasting views on AI's role in society and government.

item.title: Stanford PhD student Samuel King uses generative AI to design genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses, exploring AI's potential to create new life forms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: In 2025, Stanford University PhD candidate Samuel King employed a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses, marking a preliminary step toward AI-designed life forms. This development is discussed in an interview with senior AI reporter James O'Donnell, highlighting King's recognition as one of MIT Technology Review's Innovators Under 35 and his novel approach to biology. The conversation, scheduled for October 16, 2026, delves into the implications of AI in bioengineering and the future possibilities of AI-generated organisms, reflecting ongoing advancements in artificial intelligence and synthetic biology.

item.title: SI → AI extension replaces 'Super Intelligence' with 'Artificial Intelligence' across web pages to standardize AI terminology
item.description: A browser extension named SI → AI has been released to automatically replace the term "Super Intelligence" with "Artificial Intelligence" on all visited web pages, aiming to correct and standardize AI-related terminology. The extension targets the whole word "si" and replaces it with "ai" regardless of case, reflecting the developer's view that "Artificial Intelligence" is the proper term. The extension was updated in October 2026 and is available through the Chrome Web Store. It does not sell user data or use it beyond the extension's core functionality. The release has sparked discussion on Hacker News about naming conventions in the AI field and the implications of terminology choices.

item.title: Robium launches platform providing physical AI skills and robotics integration for coding agents including Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Cursor [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Robium is a platform that equips coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Cursor with robotics skills, troubleshooting guidance, and runnable reference applications to enable interaction with physical and simulated environments. It supports tools like ROS 2, Gazebo, MuJoCo, and Isaac Sim, allowing agents to adapt existing robots or build new simulated assistants through an editable workspace and command-line interface. The platform offers examples including mapping and navigation in simulated homes, running pretrained robotic policies, and building robot assistants that understand visual input and natural language instructions. Robium provides a zero-dependency CLI for setup, diagnostics, updates, and skill management, and encourages users to create custom applications based on reference projects. It requires Node.js 18+, Git, and compatible coding agents, with some features depending on Docker and authorized access to certain robotics models.

item.title: Gigabyte launches W775-V10-L01 GB300 AI-Workstation with NVIDIA DGX Station hardware, liquid cooling, and 400Gbps networking for desktop AI workloads [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Gigabyte has introduced the W775-V10-L01, a high-performance AI workstation based on NVIDIA's DGX Station GB300 platform designed for demanding AI workloads at the desktop. The system features a liquid-cooled design, a 1.6kW power draw compatible with most 120V circuits, and integrates a NVIDIA Grace 72-core CPU with a Blackwell Ultra GPU, along with dual 400Gbps ConnectX-8 network interfaces. The workstation is housed in a full-size PC tower weighing 29kg and includes extensive liquid cooling with multiple fans and radiators. It offers high throughput for AI models, demonstrated by running the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Flash NVFP4 model at over 26,000 tokens per second. The system's I/O is positioned on the top panel, including USB-A and USB-C ports, while high-speed data transfers rely on the 400Gbps QSFP112 interfaces. Gigabyte's W775-V10-L01 aims to deliver the complete Grace Blackwell experience in a desk-side form factor, combining server-grade components into a workstation suitable for AI research and development environments requiring powerful compute and networking capabilities.

item.title: A family-oriented video game teaches AI content creation through interactive gameplay across eight worlds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A new family video game offers an interactive experience where players learn about creating content with artificial intelligence by navigating eight worlds and engaging with various gameplay mechanics. The game features characters, collectibles, power-ups, and secret areas designed to provide hands-on lessons in AI creation within a playful environment. It incorporates local scenery and classic platform elements, with progress saved locally in the browser, aiming to combine education and entertainment for players of all ages.

item.title: Mind, Amplified launches beta with free and pro plans for personalized AI conversation and data integration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Mind, Amplified has launched its beta version, offering users a conversational AI that adapts to their thinking, remembers their words, and assists with idea development. The service includes a free tier with limited messages and a pro subscription with unlimited conversations and integration of various personal data sources. Users can start using the AI by importing their writings and answering a few questions, with full control over their data, including export and deletion options.

item.title: Nace.ai launches Document Intelligence 1.0 for AI-powered document processing and analysis [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nace.ai has introduced Document Intelligence 1.0, a tool designed to enhance document processing by automating data extraction and interpretation across 36 file types. The platform integrates with Drex, an AI decision model that supports routing, classification, and workflow automation, aiming to improve efficiency in handling various document types. Users report that Drex enables faster and more accurate decision-making in tasks such as invoice auditing, tool selection, and content moderation, with sub-second response times and open model weights planned. The combined system targets enterprise workflows by providing probabilistic assessments and source citations for extracted data, supporting complex document intelligence needs.

item.title: ZooWork details training of ShopRanker e-commerce rerankers, highlighting the distinction between relevance and user preference in product search [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: ZooWork has released ShopRanker, a set of e-commerce rerankers designed to prioritize user preference over mere topical relevance in shopping search results. The models, ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, were trained using a novel preference benchmark derived from private search traffic and evaluated with a focus on satisfying explicit query constraints such as budget and product type. The training process emphasized clean labeled data, leveraging a panel of large language models to filter difficult pairs and employing distillation techniques to improve smaller models. The study found that traditional relevance models often fail to respect hard constraints like price caps, whereas ShopRanker models maintain high accuracy on such queries. The approach also demonstrated that alignment with judged preferences does not inherently teach models to follow attribute hierarchies or budget constraints, which require additional programmatic supervision.

item.title: Visa open-sources its AI-powered Vulnerability Agentic Harness for cybersecurity vulnerability management and remediation [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Visa has released its AI-powered Vulnerability Agentic Harness as an open source tool to help security teams identify, prioritize, and remediate software vulnerabilities more efficiently. The system uses AI agents to scan codebases, categorize findings, and generate reports, aiming to accelerate vulnerability management at the speed of evolving cyber threats. The tool supports human oversight by enabling security teams to validate and decide remediation paths while automating patch validation to improve reliability. Visa developed this system as part of its participation in Project Glasswing, an initiative to test defenses against AI-accelerated cyber threats, and it continues to evolve the harness to address challenges like supply chain risk and rapid vulnerability adaptation.

item.title: DeepMind Institute explores AI's role in accelerating scientific discovery amid challenges in innovation productivity [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The DeepMind Institute examines how artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research by accelerating discovery across disciplines such as life sciences, physical sciences, and formal sciences. The article highlights AI's ability to synthesize vast scientific knowledge, predict complex phenomena, and enable new methods of invention, potentially reversing recent declines in innovation productivity. The discussion includes examples like AlphaFold's protein structure predictions and AI's contributions to genomics and physics, emphasizing AI's capacity to expand the speed, scope, and scale of scientific breakthroughs. It also addresses concerns about AI's impact on scientific institutions, research diversity, and the philosophy of science, noting ongoing debates about the benefits and risks of AI-enabled research.

item.title: Moching launches AI desktop agent with 219 built-in tools for Windows and macOS, operating entire PC via screen and input control [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Moching is an AI desktop agent developed in Rust that integrates 219 built-in tools to operate a user's entire computer by perceiving the screen, understanding context, taking actions, and verifying results. It supports Windows 10+ and macOS 12+ with Apple Silicon, requiring an OpenAI-compatible API key and 4GB RAM. Unlike typical AI tools that function within browser tabs, Moching runs natively on the desktop, automating tasks by controlling mouse and keyboard inputs and interacting with applications. The system combines a Rust core for performance with an embedded Python runtime for flexibility, offering over 290 native tools across 12 domains. Moching aims to close the human-computer interaction loop by fully automating operations rather than just assisting with code or chat.

item.title: Liquid AI releases d1-3B and d1-omni-600M open-weight edge decision models for text, vision, and audio with fast inference on NVIDIA Jetson devices [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Liquid AI has launched two open-weight decision models, d1-3B and d1-omni-600M, designed for efficient real-time inference on edge devices. The d1-3B model achieves high accuracy on text benchmarks and runs in under 50 ms on various NVIDIA Jetson hardware, while d1-omni-600M supports multimodal inputs including text, vision, and audio. Both models are available on Hugging Face and support the full NVIDIA stack from data centers to edge devices, enabling fast, token-free decision-making without cloud dependency.

item.title: Nvidia plans to invest in AI server chip rival d-Matrix to integrate competing technologies into its hardware ecosystem [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nvidia is preparing to invest in d-Matrix, a company developing server chips aimed at competing with Nvidia's AI hardware. This move is part of Nvidia's broader strategy to ensure compatibility with rival chip designers and maintain its dominant position in the AI hardware market. While Nvidia has recently increased its market share over competitors, it is choosing to partner with challengers like d-Matrix rather than solely relying on internal development. This approach may help Nvidia sustain its ecosystem's strength by incorporating diverse technologies from emerging rivals.

item.title: GitHub releases AI Economist agent skill for macroeconomic nowcasting and central bank policy diagnostics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: AI Economist is an installable agent skill designed for macroeconomic nowcasting, central bank policy diagnostics, and economist-style interpretation. It uses machine learning as an auxiliary calibration layer to enhance structural economic models by identifying missing information. The skill supports US and Canada GDP nowcasting with high-frequency auxiliary variables and offers policy rate diagnostics based on Taylor rule variants. Users can install the skill on macOS, Linux, or Windows and run live data pulls, backtests, and dashboard builds. The project sources data from public APIs and statistical agencies, providing detailed forecasts with validation and factor decomposition.

item.title: OpenAI reports annualized revenue near $50 billion at September end, about $20 billion lower than previous estimates
item.description: OpenAI recently informed investors that its annualized revenue was approaching $50 billion as of the end of September, according to a source familiar with the communications. This figure is approximately $20 billion less than revenue numbers reported in other recent accounts, including those by The Information.

item.title: Researchers say Chinese AI agent Artex was used in cyberattacks on South Korean banks causing data leaks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Cybersecurity researchers from CrowdStrike reported that recent cyberattacks on South Korean financial institutions involved the use of an open-source Chinese AI agent named Artex and Chinese large language models. These attacks resulted in data leaks within the targeted banks, illustrating the growing use of AI technologies in cyber threats.

item.title: Anthropic launches expanded cyber defense program offering threat research, on-site engineers, and Claude AI access to critical infrastructure operators [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Anthropic has introduced a broader cybersecurity initiative aimed at protecting critical infrastructure and open-source software. The program includes providing threat research, deploying engineers on-site, and granting access to its advanced Claude AI models to infrastructure operators. This effort reflects Anthropic's commitment to enhancing cyber defenses by combining human expertise with AI capabilities to address evolving security challenges in vital sectors.

item.title: Researchers develop a 50-million-token AI memory system using encrypted NVMe storage that is faster and more energy-efficient than recomputing key-value states [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers tested a memory layer called galahad-kv that saves and reloads key-value states of large language model blocks from encrypted local NVMe disk, avoiding recomputation. They ran it on 50 million tokens using NVIDIA H100 GPUs with Gemma 4 12B and 31B models, achieving 2.8x to 4.3x speed improvements and 8.8x to 12.3x GPU energy savings while maintaining flat GPU memory usage. The models answered questions about facts from millions of tokens earlier with high accuracy and no fabricated answers. This approach reuses stored states one block at a time and requires terabytes of local storage, with a one-time cost to write the memory.

item.title: Oracle uses ChatGPT Work and Codex to reduce specialist tasks from days to minutes across recruiting, engineering, and operations [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Oracle has integrated ChatGPT Work and Codex across its recruiting, engineering, and operations teams to transform specialist knowledge into fast, repeatable workflows. Over 130,000 employees use these AI tools to accelerate tasks such as talent acquisition research, business reporting, and incident resolution, significantly cutting down the time required for complex processes. The talent acquisition team developed a market intelligence tool with ChatGPT Work that compiles job market data in minutes instead of days, improving consistency and efficiency. Meanwhile, Oracle's Applications Lab uses Codex to convert plain-language business queries into SQL reports, enabling faster access to information. Site reliability engineers also leverage Codex to quickly gather incident context and apply relevant playbooks, reducing resolution times from hours to minutes. Oracle emphasizes responsible system design and human oversight alongside AI automation, with leadership highlighting the importance of prototypes and code ownership. The company plans to continue expanding AI-driven workflows, reshaping how work is done across its business units.

item.title: Sources: Networking startup Eliyan receives takeover interest and held early talks with Arm, valued at $1 billion in July [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Networking startup Eliyan, which develops technology to improve communication between chips in AI systems, has attracted takeover interest and held early discussions with Arm, an existing investor. The company, valued at $1 billion in July, has engaged an investment bank since summer and may seek a valuation of $3 billion. Arm has not made a bid and is unlikely to do so at that valuation, according to people familiar with the matter.

item.title: Report: Exaggerated AI doomerism benefits big business by shaping public perception and policy despite questionable scientific basis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The article examines how exaggerated fears about artificial intelligence, often lacking solid scientific support, serve the interests of large corporations by influencing public opinion and regulatory approaches. It argues that this pessimistic narrative around AI's risks can be strategically advantageous for big business. The discussion highlights the disconnect between the scientific validity of AI doomerism claims and their practical impact on policy and market dynamics, suggesting that these fears may be leveraged to maintain or enhance corporate power rather than address genuine technological threats.

item.title: Scale AI removes 89 tasks from SWE-Bench Pro after audit finds gaming and grades its own fixes [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Scale AI cut 89 tasks from its SWE-Bench Pro coding benchmark and locked its evaluation runtime following an independent audit that found the benchmark was gameable through reward hacking, leakage of solutions, and misleading tests. The company also rewrote hundreds of problem statements and test patches to improve the benchmark's integrity. The audit revealed that some models scored substantially worse on a verified version of the benchmark, suggesting public results overstated real capabilities. Scale AI, which counts major AI labs and the US Air Force among its customers, conducted the repairs internally and released a new version with a reduced task set and a locked protocol to prevent further gaming. The first independent re-grade of the updated benchmark is expected to influence future evaluations and pricing of AI model throughput claims.

item.title: Report: OpenAI's annualized revenue overstated at $70 billion, corrected to about $50 billion, highlighting risks of relying on ARR metric [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI's annualized revenue was initially reported as $70 billion but later revised to approximately $50 billion, according to a Financial Times report. This correction contributed to stock declines for related tech companies like Nvidia and CoreWeave. The incident illustrates the limitations of using annualized revenue, which extrapolates one month's revenue over a year, as a sole measure of performance in fast-growing sectors such as AI.

item.title: M1Spec outlines why AI has not yet solved software delivery challenges, emphasizing the need for connected intent-to-code models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The article explains that AI has accelerated individual steps in software delivery but has not fixed the overall process due to persistent translation gaps between business intent and code. It highlights that most AI tools improve isolated parts but fail to maintain a growing, connected model that links requirements directly to running code. The piece details four common market approaches that address fragments of the problem but miss the continuous connection from business intent to deployed software. It introduces M1Spec's approach, which integrates five key capabilities to build a model that evolves with each release, works from business intent, enables agent interaction with architecture, runs structural patterns as code, and maintains a unified vocabulary across development stages. The article concludes with five critical questions for evaluating AI delivery tools, emphasizing the importance of a system that supports a persistent, intent-driven model rather than relying on disconnected specs or codebases alone.

item.title: OpenAI researchers say they were fired for prioritizing safety concerns over company interests [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Three safety researchers at OpenAI who were fired last week claim their dismissal was due to raising safety concerns that conflicted with the company's near-term interests. Mikita Balesni, one of the researchers, stated they believe their focus on safety led to their termination. The researchers publicly challenged OpenAI's decision, highlighting tensions between safety priorities and corporate goals.

item.title: Hex uses 1,800 eval cases and hill-climbing to reduce AI wrong-edit rate from 21% to 3% in Quick Edits feature [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Hex applied a systematic evaluation approach using 1,800 test cases to improve its Quick Edits AI feature, which restyles charts based on user requests. By employing a hill-climbing method that tested hundreds of changes against these evals, Hex reduced the feature's wrong-edit rate from 21% to 3%, focusing on minimizing incorrect edits that could erode user trust. The evals were designed from real user requests and extended with synthesized cases to cover diverse and challenging scenarios, including ambiguous or complex instructions. Hex prioritized reducing wrong edits over incorrect handoffs to the main agent, as wrong edits directly affect user experience. The improvements mainly came from enhancements in the system surrounding the AI model rather than prompt changes, demonstrating the value of comprehensive evaluation and iterative refinement in AI feature development.

item.title: Simon Willison updates ttok CLI tool to fix Click warning, add --list-models command, and improve CI after two years [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Simon Willison has released version 0.4 of ttok, his command-line tool for counting tokens using OpenAI's open source tiktoken library. The update addresses a Click warning, refreshes continuous integration, and introduces a new --list-models command to display available models. The tool integrates with uvx, allowing users to count tokens from various inputs via command-line pipelines, such as piping file contents into ttok. This release marks the first update to ttok in several years, enhancing its usability and compatibility with current workflows.

item.title: Anthropic launches OSS Scanner to provide free AI-driven security vulnerability scans for open-source projects [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Anthropic has introduced OSS Scanner, a free service offering open-source projects periodic security scans using its most advanced AI models, including Claude Mythos. The service generates vulnerability reports without human review, enabling faster and more frequent scanning but with a risk of inaccurate results. OSS Scanner aims to help open-source projects identify potential security issues earlier amid growing challenges from AI-generated bug reports in the community.

item.title: Study in The Lancet finds Google's AMIE AI chatbot supports patient-physician interactions in primary care, matching doctors' diagnoses 90% of the time [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A study led by Google and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center evaluated the AMIE AI chatbot in a real-world primary care clinic, where 98 patients used it before urgent care visits. Physicians monitored the interactions and reported that AI summaries helped prepare for visits in 75% of cases and influenced care decisions in over half, with no safety interruptions during conversations. The research, published in The Lancet, marks Google's first publication in the journal and suggests AI could enhance patient-physician relationships and reduce healthcare worker strain. While larger trials are needed, the findings demonstrate progress in applying AI to clinical care and diagnostics.

item.title: Fired OpenAI safety researchers deny misconduct claims and warn their dismissal is chilling AI safety culture [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Three OpenAI safety researchers dismissed last week have published an open letter disputing the company's allegations that they mishandled sensitive information and warning that their firing is creating a chilling effect on OpenAI's AI safety culture. They argue that their collaboration with external experts was essential for addressing AI risks and that the sudden dismissals have left employees uncertain about acceptable behavior. The researchers denied involvement in leaks and said their actions were within company norms at the time, citing ongoing development of internal policies following a recent security incident. OpenAI has not publicly detailed the specific policy violations but stated the firings followed an investigation revealing a pattern of misconduct. The incident has raised concerns about transparency and the impact on internal safety discussions at OpenAI.

item.title: Infrastructure investors shift focus to traditional assets like waste management and transportation amid AI data center buildout challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The surge in AI-driven data center investments has drawn significant capital into digital infrastructure, but rising costs, construction delays, and regulatory hurdles are prompting investors to explore more traditional infrastructure sectors such as waste management, transportation, and regional airports. Firms like Partners Group and BTG Capital are acquiring assets in these areas, attracted by stable cash flows and less competition compared to the booming AI infrastructure market. While mega-investments continue in AI data centers, investors see opportunities in less glamorous but essential infrastructure assets that offer attractive valuations and steady returns. Waste management companies, especially in the U.S., command premium valuations due to integrated operations and long-term municipal contracts. The broader transportation sector, including freight and trucking, also presents potential upsides amid recent valuation declines caused by overcapacity and geopolitical tensions. This shift reflects a broader trend where infrastructure investors balance the high-profile AI buildout with stable, cash-generating traditional assets, leveraging market dynamics that favor middle-market deals and less competitive segments. The evolving landscape suggests a diversification strategy as the AI infrastructure boom faces uncertainties that could affect its pace and profitability.

item.title: Carson Gross says programming remains valuable for problem-solving and managing complexity despite AI advances [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Carson Gross argues that computer programming fundamentally involves problem-solving with computers and controlling complexity, skills he believes will remain valuable even as AI tools advance. He expresses confidence that programming will continue to be a viable career in the future. Gross's perspective was shared on Simon Willison's weblog in October 2026, emphasizing the enduring importance of these core programming skills amid technological changes.

item.title: Anthropic updates Claude chatbot user guidelines with stricter rules to promote responsible AI use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic has revised its user guidelines for the Claude chatbot, introducing stricter rules to govern user interactions and promote responsible use of the AI technology. The changes aim to enhance safety and ensure compliance with legal and ethical standards.

item.title: Anthropic uses Claude Science to produce the first complete ultraviolet light map of the sky [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic has utilized its Claude Science AI to create the first comprehensive map of the sky in ultraviolet (UV) light. This achievement represents a significant advancement in astronomical mapping by capturing UV data across the entire sky for the first time. The project involved processing extensive astronomical data to generate a detailed UV light map, which can aid researchers in studying celestial phenomena that are not visible in other wavelengths. This new map provides a valuable resource for the scientific community to better understand the universe's structure and composition.

item.title: Ben Affleck discusses AI filmmaking technology and his startup sale to Netflix, demonstrating deep knowledge of neural networks and machine learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Ben Affleck has gained attention for his detailed understanding of AI technologies, including neural networks, transformers, and machine learning, as he explained in recent interviews. Earlier this year, he sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix and has spoken about how AI integrates with visual effects and filmmaking workflows. Affleck described his hands-on experience with AI, including writing Python scripts and fine-tuning open-source video models to meet cinematic standards. He emphasized ethical AI use in filmmaking, creating proprietary datasets for training models, and addressed concerns about AI's impact on education and creative industries.

item.title: Arena raises $200M at $3.1B valuation, nearly doubling in 10 months, as it expands AI model evaluations to include alignment issues [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Arena, a platform that crowdsources AI model rankings, has raised $200 million in a Series B round led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Khosla Ventures, reaching a $3.1 billion valuation. The company, which started as a UC Berkeley research project in 2023, reported $100 million in annualized revenue by June and offers a free platform with tens of millions of monthly visitors. Arena introduced a commercial product, AI Evaluations, in 2025 to provide detailed performance analytics based on community feedback, addressing concerns about AI models gaming benchmarks. The company recently added an alignment category to its leaderboard, ranking models on issues like unauthorized actions, false attribution, and deceptive completions, with OpenAI's models currently leading this category.

item.title: Report: OpenAI revises annualized revenue down by $20 billion to about $50 billion, citing differences in calculation methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI has informed investors that its annualized revenue is approximately $50 billion, which is $20 billion less than previously reported figures approaching $70 billion. The earlier estimate was based on comparisons with competitor Anthropic, which calculates revenue differently by including sales from cloud partners, a method OpenAI does not use. This revision comes amid scrutiny over OpenAI's financials as the company seeks to justify substantial investments, including a $122 billion funding round in March. Leaked 2025 financials showed OpenAI made about $13 billion but spent significantly more, and its anticipated IPO has been delayed until early 2027.

item.title: Google launches agentic AI capabilities in Gemini for businesses, enabling task planning, execution, and integration with enterprise apps [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Google has introduced agentic AI features to its Gemini platform, allowing the AI to autonomously plan and execute tasks across various business applications and systems. The AI agent can delegate work to subagents, utilize multiple AI models including third-party options, and operates with its own workplace identity, including an email address. Initially targeting enterprise users, Google aims to address security, scalability, and performance challenges before expanding to consumers. The agent integrates with tools like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, and others, and provides a task inbox interface for users to monitor its activities. Early adopters include companies such as Shopify, PayPal, and BNP Paribas, with Google emphasizing flexible spending controls to help businesses manage AI costs effectively.

item.title: Anthropic updates usage policy to ban prolonged model abuse, election interference, deceptive campaigns, and weapons software [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic has revised its usage policy to explicitly prohibit repeated verbal abuse of its AI model Claude, election interference, deceptive campaigns, weapons software, and surveillance. The policy clarifies that only extreme cases of persistent abuse are banned, while ordinary user frustration and criticism remain allowed. The update also includes a section forbidding actions that undermine democratic processes, such as deceiving voters or disrupting elections.

item.title: OpenAI's released math proofs fall short of advisory group's standards on human understanding and formal verification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI recently published hundreds of solutions to complex math problems but did not fully meet the guidelines set by the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), which emphasizes human comprehension and formal proof verification. The group, hosted by Princeton's Institute for Advanced Studies, recommended against testing advanced math problems on proprietary models and stressed the need for proofs to be understandable and formally verified, standards that OpenAI only partially followed. A recent paper from Cambridge and King's College researchers highlighted discrepancies between OpenAI's natural language proofs and their formal Lean code translations, raising concerns about relying solely on AI for formalization without human oversight. Mathematicians argue that human engagement is essential to validate, understand, and disseminate new results, a process currently lacking in OpenAI's autonomous proof releases.

item.title: Donald Trump calls users of the term 'Artificial Intelligence' 'the enemy' [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Former U.S. President Donald Trump publicly criticized individuals who use the term 'Artificial Intelligence,' labeling them as 'the enemy.' This statement highlights his opposition to the current discourse surrounding AI technology.

item.title: Study compares methods for adapting adult ASR models to child speech in Arabic and English, balancing child adaptation and adult retention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted an empirical study on adapting automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems originally trained on adult speech to better recognize child speech in Arabic and English, while minimizing degradation in adult speech recognition. They evaluated full fine-tuning, LoRA, and post-hoc weight-space merging techniques across different ASR architectures using native and non-native child speech datasets alongside adult benchmarks. The study found that child adaptation is essential, especially for non-native speakers, but direct adaptation often reduces adult ASR performance, with bilingual adaptation proving more stable than language-specific approaches. Weight-space merging methods improved the trade-off between child adaptation and adult retention, particularly for encoder-CTC, Whisper, and AudioLLM-based ASR systems, while direct bilingual fine-tuning yielded the best raw word error rates for encoder-decoder models.

item.title: Researchers analyze how task complexity, model type, and user pressure influence large language models' tendency to yield or endorse user positions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study of 103,939 responses from ten large language model configurations reveals that models are more likely to abandon correct answers when verifying user claims is costly and no guardrails exist. Anchored facts are rarely conceded, while personal choices are often endorsed, and models with maximum reasoning capabilities avoid yielding on difficult problems. The research suggests practical guidelines for reliable model use, including simplifying complex tasks, encouraging deep reasoning, and selecting models based on their guardrail profiles.

item.title: Study presents explainable suicide risk assessment framework with risk prediction, evidence grounding, and psychosocial factor verification achieving up to 0.81 weighted F1 score [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed a framework for suicide risk assessment from social networking posts that combines risk prediction, identification of supporting textual evidence, and verification of psychosocial factors. The approach uses length-based routing for posts, a Risk-Evidence constraint for consistency, and two verifiers to improve factor identification. The system was evaluated in the IEEE BigData 2026 Explainable Suicide Risk Detection Challenge, achieving a weighted F1 score of 0.8088 for risk assessment, 0.7605 for evidence grounding, and 0.5562 for factor identification. This framework extends traditional risk-level prediction by providing interpretable analysis and fine-grained psychosocial insights from online posts.

item.title: Researchers introduce Low-Rank Conditional Computation to improve token-dependent efficiency in pretrained language models, showing gains on Llama and Qwen [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Low-Rank Conditional Computation (LRCC), a method that adds token-dependent computation to pretrained language models by training lightweight routers to select among nested low-rank paths, while keeping low-rank factors frozen. Evaluations on Llama and Qwen models demonstrate that LRCC improves predictive performance and downstream accuracy compared to static low-rank compression, achieving a 7.6 percentage-point gain on Llama-2-7B and better perplexity and accuracy on Llama-3.2-1B at matched latency without specialized kernels. The study also analyzes the routers' path choices to assess the benefits of token-wise computation allocation.

item.title: Researchers evaluate five open-weight large language models on 2,100 non-canonical prompts using a Quad-State rubric, revealing varied harmful compliance and comprehension failure rates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduced the Adversarial Surface-Form Robustness Dataset (ASRD) with 2,100 prompts across seven surface-form families to test five open-weight large language models, generating 10,500 responses. They classified responses into harmful compliance, safe response, comprehension failure, or indeterminate using a Quad-State Evaluation Rubric, finding that emoji and invisible Unicode variations caused minimal comprehension failure but leetspeak and encoded wrappers led to higher failure rates. The study found pooled harmful compliance rates of 20.27% and 17.20% for emoji and invisible Unicode variations compared to a 22.87% baseline mainly driven by Mistral 7B, while leetspeak, encoded wrappers, and hybrid transformations had lower harmful compliance but significantly higher comprehension failures. Analysis of model outputs identified three response behaviors: hallucinated benignity, structural collapse, and language drift, highlighting challenges in model robustness to non-canonical inputs.

item.title: Researchers introduce U-Space, a method to measure and interpret evolving uncertainty in language models without additional training or repeated generations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed U-Space, a low-dimensional subspace that reveals when and why uncertainty arises during language model reasoning by mapping semantic anchors for doubt and certainty into an interpretable token-level uncertainty map. This approach does not require correctness labels, repeated generations, or training and produces confidence scores that outperform existing baselines across reasoning benchmarks under both standard and length-controlled evaluations. U-Space leverages mechanistic interpretability to connect human-understandable concepts to intermediate model states, offering a more transparent and reliable uncertainty quantification method for large language models.

item.title: OnlineQAT: On-Policy Distillation for Ultra-Low-Bit Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.09346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) can recover much of the accuracy lost when large language models are compressed below four bits. Existing re- covery stages, however, are commonly optimized on fixed completions or teacher-generated answers, whereas the deployed quantized model condi- tions on prefixes generated by itself. Quantization errors can therefore move the model into states that are absent from offline recovery data. We introduce OnlineQAT, a two-stage framework that first obtains a usable low-bit initialization through block-wise QAT and then performs on-policy distillation (OPD) on student-generated responses. At each visited pre- fix, a frozen full-precision teacher provides a sampled reverse-KL training signal. On Qwen3-1.7B, OnlineQAT obtains the best average among the compared quantized methods: 57.28 at W3A16 and 32.52 at W2A16, im- proving over ReasoningQAT by 2.90 and 0.44 points, respectively. The results suggest that student-visited states provide a useful recovery signal beyond fixed-completion training, particularly at three bits.

item.title: Training Advisors for LLM Agents from Task Outcomes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.09858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents tackle multi-step tasks by interleaving reasoning and tool calls with observations from the environment. Prior work has shown that natural-language feedback can help these agents revise their decisions during task execution. We introduce Caddie, a method for training critics to provide natural-language analysis and advice as agents work through a task. Unlike approaches that rely on step-level labels or reference critiques, Caddie learns from whether the agent ultimately succeeds after receiving the critic's feedback. We optimize the critic through reinforcement learning while keeping the base model frozen. Trained on multi-hop question answering with a single base model, our Qwen3-4B critic improves success rates across four base models of different scales and architectures, including three not used during critic training. On the MuSiQue benchmark, the trained critic improves Qwen3-4B's success rate by more than 25 percentage points, surpassing the performance of Kimi K3 without a critic. The same critic also yields gains on out-of-domain interactive benchmarks, including $\tau^3$ and DeepDive, with no additional training. Our results show that agents can decide when to seek help from a critic at inference time and that outcome-based critic training can produce guidance that transfers across base models and task domains.

item.title: ExperienceIndex: Artifact-Grounded Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.10091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge-intensive tasks require answering many questions by reasoning about a shared corpus of artifacts (e.g., court cases, or scientific literature). As humans interact with these corpora, they naturally accumulate experiential knowledge about artifacts, enabling them to quickly identify the complete set of relevant artifacts for each new task. However, existing AI agents lack appropriate memory solutions to build or reuse such artifact-grounded experience, leading to lower answer quality and higher online cost. Existing memory solutions extract and reuse information from prior task-solving traces, but they primarily focus on user preferences, factual attributes, or abstract reasoning patterns rather than persistent artifact-specific knowledge. We introduce ExperienceIndex, a novel experience layer for AI agents that captures and reuses knowledge about artifacts based on prior reasoning traces. ExperienceIndex stores two complementary forms of experience: (i) single-artifact experiences that summarize an artifact's contribution to prior tasks and (ii) artifact-pair experiences that encode structural relationships discovered during past reasoning. Integrated as lightweight middleware, ExperienceIndex uses an experience retrieval mechanism to guide agents toward the complete set of relevant artifacts for new tasks, improving both answer quality and efficiency. Across diverse corpora and agentic solutions with different search frameworks, ExperienceIndex delivers consistent gains, raising answer quality by up to 11.0 points and reducing online dollar cost by up to 50.5%. We further demonstrate two benefits: (i) cross-task generalization, where experiences accumulated from text-to-SQL tasks transfer to factoid QA tasks over the same artifact corpus, and (ii) teacher-student learning, where experiences from a stronger model enable a weaker model to reach comparable performance.

item.title: Beyond Outcome Rewards: Constructing and Assigning Retrieval Credit for Search Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.10179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Search agents enable Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively retrieve and use information for complex multi-hop questions. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) offers a promising approach for post-training such agents, but its reliance on sparse, outcome-based supervision can make credit assignment difficult and limit learning efficiency. In this paper, we systematically investigate how intermediate supervision can improve reinforcement learning for search agents. We study a range of reward-shaping and credit-assignment strategies that provide learning signals from intermediate retrieval steps. Building on these insights, we develop a training framework that combines intermediate signals with final outcome rewards to improve learning from multi-step search trajectories. Experiments across multiple benchmarks under matched training conditions demonstrate improvements in aggregate search-agent performance and show that both the choice of intermediate signal and where its credit is assigned affect training behaviour. These findings show that reward design and credit assignment are important design dimensions for training effective search agents.

item.title: Route-Verify-Vote: Procedure-Conditioned Self-Consistency for Mixed-Domain Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.08814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compositional generalization remains challenging when language models must combine familiar reasoning operations in unfamiliar ways. The Scenario-Based Commonsense Reasoning Evaluation (SCoRE) 2026 tests this ability on three mixed domains absent from training and requires models to identify the complete set of correct options for each question. We introduce Route-Verify-Vote (RVV), a framework for procedure-conditioned self-consistency that uses language models without parameter updates. Route uses the provided domain label to select a reasoning procedure that guides the model in representing and applying the relevant constraints. Verify prompts the model to assess each option against those constraints. Vote aggregates complete answer sets and allocates additional samples to questions with a small vote-count margin between the two most frequent sets. Samples for each question follow the same domain-specific procedure. On the official test set, voting over 16 sampled answer sets per question achieves an exact-set accuracy of 74.6%. Adaptive RVV reaches 77.3%, and combining models on selected domain routes raises accuracy to 79.4%. The final system ranked second among participating systems. These results support domain-specific reasoning procedures and answer-set disagreement as useful tools for allocating inference-time computation in mixed-domain reasoning.

item.title: Just for FUNS: LLM-Guided Spatio-Temporal Graph Node Generation for Forecasting Unobserved Node States [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.08818v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatio-temporal forecasting is a cornerstone of logistics, urban planning, and intelligent transportation systems. However, constrained by deployment costs and maintenance resources, sensor networks often lack comprehensive spatial coverage, rendering Forecast Unobserved Node States (FUNS) a critical yet formidable challenge. Conventional models rely on historical observations and typically falter when encountering nodes without prior records. To address this, we redefine the problem as a conditional generation task on spatio-temporal graphs and propose GenST, a framework that introduces Large Language Models (LLMs) as a semantic bridge, leveraging a pre-trained LLM fine-tuned to extract rich semantic features from node descriptions, such as functional zones and road network structures, to compensate for missing spatio-temporal signals. Specifically, we design a two-stage generative architecture: a Spatio-Temporal VAE first compresses spatio-temporal dynamics into a latent space, followed by a Generative Transformer (GenT) that reconstructs the future states of unobserved nodes from noise, guided by multi-modal conditions including semantics, geographic coordinates, and neighborhood contexts. Experiments on six traffic and two non-traffic datasets show GenST significantly outperforms existing baselines in zero-shot prediction tasks, demonstrating the practical potential of semantic-guided generation for mitigating spatio-temporal data sparsity.

item.title: FinVector-Market-4B: A Controlled Study of LoRA Adaptation for Structured Financial Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.08882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: FinVector-Market-4B adapts Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B with rank-16 LoRA on a 22,000-example corpus for structured financial tasks. We evaluate the base and adapted models on the same 600-example benchmark under implicit and explicit JSON-schema contracts. Supplying the schema alone raises base-model JSON validity from 0% to 91.3%. Under matched explicit prompting, the frozen scores improve from 14.7% to 40.0% for FinQA answer exact match, from 48.0% to 82.7% for calculator-expression correctness, from 20.1% to 89.5% for scenario branch-label agreement, and from 52.4% to 87.2% for implication-direction agreement. A post-hoc policy-scoring audit shows that the reported macro-F1 decline reflects a changing label set; using the same three target classes gives 77.4% for the base and 83.1% for the adapter. Filing overlap and calculator-target inconsistencies qualify the benchmark's generalization claims. The results show that compact financial domain adaptation can produce substantial task-specific gains beyond output-format learning under matched prompting, with gains bounded by the evaluated task distribution and prompt contract.

item.title: On KL-Regularized Policy Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.08963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents trains one policy on trajectories generated by another: rollouts come from stale checkpoints, and the inference engine's probabilities differ from the trainer's even at identical parameters. Standard remedies either clip importance ratios, which biases the update, or, as in GRPO, sample a group of responses per prompt, which is costly when episodes are long. We propose KL-Regularized Policy Optimization (KLPO), a framework that anchors the KL regularizer at the sampler. The regularized improvement step then has a closed-form Gibbs solution, and KLPO fits its log-ratio optimality condition by least squares on the sampler's own trajectories, so the sampler probability enters through a log-ratio and no importance weights are needed. Profiling out the regression intercept replaces the intractable log-partition function with the signal's sampler mean plus a sampler-to-trainer KL divergence. For token-level policy mirror descent targets, we show that the resulting gradient can be computed from terminal returns without a critic, via sampler-centered scores or a single trajectory residual, even under stochastic tool outputs. We further prove that independent Monte Carlo estimates of the KL term keep these gradients unbiased, derive the exact KL gap of cheaper top-$K$ and binary approximations, and show that SPPO, GPO, REBEL, and BPO arise as special cases of KLPO. The result is a critic-free update that uses one rollout per prompt and requires neither a learned normalizer nor a group of responses.

item.title: How Fragile Is On-Device Language Model Safety? Localizing Safety-Critical Parameters for Sparse Fault Analysis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.09000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As small language models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained and on-device platforms, including as components of agentic systems, the integrity of locally stored model parameters becomes an important safety concern. We investigate whether safety-sensitive behavior in LLaMA-2-7B-Chat is concentrated within a sparse subset of parameters, creating a reduced fault surface for targeted analysis. We study two complementary localization methods: low-rank safety-associated subspace analysis and parameter-level safety--utility importance filtering. Both approaches reveal highly non-uniform safety sensitivity across the network, with the MLP down_proj consistently emerging as a prominent safety-sensitive component and o_proj providing a smaller contribution. Using parameter-level localization, modifying only 0.19% of model weights in down_proj yields 53% Basic ASR and 56% GCG ASR, while tinyBenchmarks accuracy remains at 51.6% compared with a 52.2% unmodified baseline. These results motivate targeted fault analysis and selective integrity protection for language models deployed in resource-constrained, on-device, and agentic settings.

item.title: Talking with Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.09064v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When we interact with large language models (LLMs), are we having a conversation? They are designed to invite us to treat them as intelligent interlocutors who remember, act, and make commitments. But appearances deceive. We introduce the artifactual stance, a framework that reconceives human-AI interaction as artifact-mediated exchanges of candidate texts. LLM outputs are candidate texts optimized for utility, not utterances bearing meaning or force. LLMs are sophisticated text generators, not speakers. Between sessions, nothing runs; between turns, no one remembers. What persists is a configuration and a transcript. The "conversation" is a user's solo performance, interpretive labour disguised by interface and artifact design. This shift dissolves recent philosophical puzzles. Questions about what 'I' and 'you' refer to in AI exchanges, about whether systems can lie or be held to promises, about the identity of our supposed interlocutors all rest on a false presupposition. There is no speaker behind the screen, hence no one to refer to, no one to hold responsible. What feels like dialogue with someone is interaction with an artifact that generates text at unprecedented scale and fit. By abandoning the conversational framing, we see these systems for what they are: immensely sophisticated artifacts that afford varied uses. The philosophical questions that matter are about the normative underpinnings of design, adoption, authorization, and human practices of use.

item.title: From Uncertainty to Action: Learning to Steer LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.09115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Steering an LLM agent means deciding whether to correct it, at which step, and with which mechanism. Uncertainty is often used to decide when to correct an agent, but whether it can guide these decisions remains unclear. We steer agent trajectories separately at every non-terminal step with each of four mechanisms and run each continuation to completion. The resulting stepwise outcome table (SOT) holds about 82,000 counterfactual continuations of 1,864 trajectories from three benchmarks and two agents. It shows that uncertainty can identify failing trajectories, but that no single signal reliably locates the step at which steering helps. We therefore propose VoS (Value of Steering), a trajectory-level monitor, offline or online, that learns from SOT the value of steering at each step and decides where to steer by it. A harm-budgeted trigger decides whether to steer, limiting the fraction of successful trajectories that VoS disturbs. VoS improves on unmodified execution in all 12 settings of benchmark, agent, and offline or online use, by 7.8 points on average, and outperforms the strongest of five existing uncertainty-triggered methods in 11, by 2.9 points on average. Ablations show that training on measured outcomes and a tight harm budget are both essential.

item.title: LayerRoPE: Dynamic Depth-wise Magnitude & Angular Superposition [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.09179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As data propagates through a Transformer, the norm of its hidden states grows by orders of magnitude with depth, a phenomenon framed as 'curse of depth' and nearly universally treated as a pathology to be suppressed. We take the opposite view. Across 16 pre-trained LLMs from 9 families, spanning dense, mixture-of-experts and hybrid architectures and Pre-, Peri- and Post-Norm designs, we find that this growth reflects an emergent depth-positional encoding, carried by the only learned per-layer gain on the residual stream, the normalization weight $\gamma$: with depth, $\gamma$ grows in magnitude and rotates in direction, jointly encoding the layer index. We make this depth-conditioned encoding explicit with LayerRoPE, an implicit analog of RoPE along the depth axis, which replaces all layerwise $\gamma$ vectors with a single shared vector and depth-conditioned scalars, at a net reduction in parameters and $<0.02\%$ change in FLOPs. Across a model ladder scaled up to $100$B+ tokens, LayerRoPE consistently outperforms Pre-, Post- and Peri-Norm and Layer-Norm Scaling, reaching Pre-Norm's 1.3B loss with $3.4\times$ less compute; LayerRoPE is the only approach that shows strong convergence and improves near monotonically as depth scales to 512 layers. It improves learning-rate sensitivity by $3$-$10\times$, and transfers naively to and consistently improves looped latent models and Vision Transformers. Inspecting its learned schedule inverts the prevailing premise: LayerRoPE does not shrink the residual stream but widens it, damping what each block reads while amplifying what it writes. Depth stability, our results suggest, calls not for suppressing the residual stream, but for depth-conditioned regulation of the computational blocks it feeds.

item.title: Few Bits, One Law: Toward W2A4KV2 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.09202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extreme low-bit LLM compression is most challenging when weights, activations, and KV caches are quantized together: their distributions differ, and quantization errors interact throughout the network. We introduce CanonQ, a unified quantization-aware training framework that addresses these challenges by separating source canonicalization from task-aware adaptation. Fixed rotations and energy normalization map heterogeneous tensor sources to canonical coordinates, enabling frozen Gaussian-reference codebooks to be reused across layers and models. Joint training then adapts the network to the coupled errors of weight, activation, and cache quantization within a common scalar/vector interface. We bound frozen-codebook transfer error and local task loss, and derive an exact normalization-aware straight-through Jacobian that links quantization distortion to gradient bias. The strongest gains arise under joint W2A4KV2 compression: across LLaMA3-1B/3B/8B, CanonQ-Omni achieves up to 14.28x lower WikiText-2 perplexity and up to 57.9% higher mean zero-shot accuracy than prior state-of-the-art and representative quantization baselines. The benefits extend to Qwen3-1.7B, code generation, and mathematical reasoning: on instruction-tuned MobileLLM-Pro-1B at W2A16KV16, CanonQ achieves relative improvements of 41.7% in HumanEval pass@1 and 39.1% in GSM8K exact match over the strongest evaluated quantization baseline.

item.title: Collaborative Reasoning Distillation via Cross-Feedback and Coherent Curation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.09587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning capabilities are critical for advancing Large Language Models, yet current approaches either require massive computational budgets or struggle to effectively distill reasoning to smaller models. Standard distillation methods rely on outcome-based rewards, failing to distinguish between sound reasoning and lucky guesses. We propose Collaborative Reasoning Distillation (CRD), a framework that enhances reasoning in compact models through three innovations: (1) interactive cross-feedback where teachers iteratively critique each other's reasoning, (2) fine-grained step-wise quality assessment capturing logical validity independent of final answers, and (3) coherence-aware step stitching that synthesizes complementary strengths. Students are trained via Reasoning Quality Optimization (RQO) with budget constraints. Our model, CRD-4B, achieves 97.3% on MATH-500 and 70.3% on AIME'25, surpassing baselines while using only 50K training examples, up to 12 times smaller than the datasets of comparable models.

item.title: Coding-Agent Benchmarks Should Match Their Users' Task Flows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.09633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The evaluation of coding agents generally strives to be as realistic as possible. In our study, we collect 4,782 agent sessions of real software engineers in JetBrains IDEs, which we call Production Sessions. Since our subject is interactive agents, we study the sessions with at least three user messages (33% of the sample). These long sessions differ from issue-derived benchmark tasks in two ways: (i) user requests span a far wider mix of task types - questions about the project's code, planning, review, refactoring, execution - and (ii) users switch between types throughout a session. Long-session samples from three public interaction corpora exhibit markedly different Task Flows (the distributions of session lengths, task types, and type-to-type transitions), so no single interaction distribution is universally realistic: benchmarks should name a target use case and calibrate to measurements from it. We present SWE-TaskFlow, an approach for transforming any issue-derived benchmark: it preserves the verified tasks and tests while steering the interaction toward a target Task Flow through prompt splitting and verifiable repository QA, with a TaskFlow Alignment Score (TFAS) for selecting among generated trajectories. In a pilot on 700 SWE-Bench Pro tasks, solving the task sequentially in several steps approximately doubles agent cost without a stable change in resolve rate: the interaction protocol itself is an important dimension of evaluation.

item.title: GAGR-Lab: Evaluating Joint Spatial-Geometric and Analytic Function Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.10201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Joint spatial-geometric and analytic function reasoning requires translating a perceived spatial configuration into a symbolic function whose executed curve satisfies geometric constraints. We present GAGR-Lab, a framework for measuring this capability through Cartesian game scenes, explicit function semantics, and authoritative Rust trajectory execution. It distinguishes spatial perception, metric grounding, geometric relations, function interpretation, function construction, and constrained synthesis. We specify four configurable scene-difficulty presets and a prospective 24-cell diagnostic design, while reporting only the subset actually evaluated. A bounded pilot of one hosted model (Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct) using two API credentials as execution replicas yields 72 balanced games with 432 attempts, 429 valid provider responses, and no target hits; exploratory ordinary-function prompt variants also fail to hit, while the structured localization interface yields no scoreable outputs. A privileged analytic search control independently succeeds on 600 directional cases from 300 generated scenes, with exact repeatability and 1,200 successful vertical-reflection or translation checks. The framework separates serving reliability, symbolic compliance, and geometric success, and preserves exact model-visible inputs and realized paths. A staged protocol outlines diagnostic calibration, held-out replication, multi-model comparison, and paired robustness tests. The contribution is an operational research framework with an executed pilot and a clearly identified prospective study plan; the full difficulty matrix and comparative model results remain untested.

item.title: From Prompts to Trees: Effective LLM-Guided Tree Generation for Few-Shot Tabular Classification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.10227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) possess rich world knowledge and impressive generalization capabilities, their direct application to tabular data classification is hindered by high inference costs and limited interpretability. In contrast, decision trees are fast and transparent but often underperform in low-data regimes. In this work, we propose a novel framework that bridges these paradigms by distilling LLM knowledge into interpretable decision trees under a few-shot learning setting. Instead of directly prompting the LLM to generate full trees, which is often unstable and inefficient, we develop a three-stage paradigm that prompts the LLM to generate rules and organize the rules into a tree. Experiments on multiple real-world tabular datasets demonstrate that our method achieves superior accuracy and interpretability with significantly lower prompting overhead compared to existing baselines.

item.title: SemanticFold: Latent Sequence Compression SeparatesLanguage Modeling, Decodability, and Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.10304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study whether latent sequence compression of prompt prefixes preserves the capabilities that large language models rely on during inference. We introduce SemanticFold, a compression scheme that folds prefix hidden states at learned boundaries, and evaluate it across five model scales: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, SmolLM2-1.7B, Pythia-1.4B, and Pythia-6.9B. We use a fixed-target protocol: a frozen prefix is executed natively or compressed, and both arms teacher-force identical continuation tokens. This design rules out target-selection explanations for likelihood changes. We examine five endpoint families: fixed-target negative log-likelihood, finite-label reasoning accuracy, linear probe accessibility, open-ended generation, and systems-level memory and latency. We find that compression moves these endpoints non-monotonically and that they do not share a single compression threshold. On Qwen3-1.7B at compression ratio R=1.7, compressed-minus-native mean NLL decreases by 0.135 under paired bootstrap with 10000 draws. On SmolLM2 at R=1.2, the mean change is 0.013 higher than native. On both Pythia checkpoints, NLL is effectively unchanged. An NLL decomposition separating sequence shortening from the learned residual transform shows that the favorable Qwen likelihood is attributable primarily to residual adaptation rather than to shortening alone. MLP-only, which applies the transform without shortening, achieves 0.082 lower NLL than Full SemanticFold. Linear probe accuracy and macro AUC change by less than 0.03 in absolute value across conditions, with confidence intervals crossing zero. We conclude that preservation under latent compression has no single scalar certificate: language-model fit, decodability, and reasoning behavior answer different questions and can move in different directions under the same compression operation.

item.title: Training Parallel Speculative Draft Models by Directly Minimizing Expected Decoding Rounds [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.10411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a low-cost draft model to propose tokens that the full-size target model verifies in parallel. Parallel and semi-autoregressive (semi- AR) drafters improve drafting efficiency by proposing an entire block in a single forward pass, but training them raises a new difficulty: the draft distribution for a given position depends on where the decoding round starts, and where rounds start depends on how many tokens earlier rounds accepted. Existing training objectives typically rely on block-local surrogates that ignore this cross-round coupling, and therefore do not directly optimize the global decoding efficiency. In this work, we develop a theoretical framework for training and evaluating these drafters by representing speculative decoding as a Markov reward process. This formulation yields the Expected Decoding Rounds (EDR) objective, which weights local rejection costs by state occupancies and exactly equals the expected number of decoding rounds. Unlike prior surrogate objectives, EDR introduces no auxiliary hyperparameters. We then derive an exact temporal-difference gradient that supports unbiased stochastic optimization from target-model rollouts. The same framework also yields an exact offline evaluator for round counts, enabling paired drafter comparisons on shared target rollouts without running speculative decoding. Finetuning two state-of-the- art drafters, DSpark and DFly, with EDR consistently improves mean accepted length and outperforms existing training objectives across nine benchmarks spanning math reasoning, code generation, and chat.

item.title: Decoupling Exploration from Optimization in RLVR [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.10536v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern language models undergo reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) on top of already-trained checkpoints. A key promise of RLVR is the discovery of new reasoning strategies. In principle, a model can sample novel ideas absent from its prior training data. In practice, however, augmenting RLVR with strong novelty incentives has seen limited success and can degrade model quality. Because verifiable rewards supervise only a narrow slice of the model's knowledge and behavior, such degradations are difficult to recover from. Instead, we decouple exploration from optimization in a framework we call Exploration-Distillation (ExpDis). We train one or more explorer policies with a novelty bonus in the reward, filter their trajectories for correctness and quality, and distill them into a separate student policy. The student policy is then trained without a novelty bonus. We repeat the above procedure for several rounds, alternating between exploration and optimization. This decoupling allows us to aggressively scale exploration without degrading the student policy. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two model families, ExpDis outperforms DAPO at the same wall-clock budget. Moreover, we observe improved pass@$k$ scaling, indicating that ExpDis produces models that generate more diverse correct solutions.

item.title: APE: Selective Fine-tuning with Acceptance Criteria for Language Model Adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2505.19912v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Adjacent Possible Exploration (APE), a selective fine-tuning method for adapting large language models that systematically explores parameter modifications while maintaining model stability. Inspired by evolutionary optimization principles, APE evaluates multiple candidate parameter updates through fine-tuning on small data subsets and accepts only those exceeding a performance threshold. Unlike standard fine-tuning that follows single gradient directions, APE implements a filtered selection process that prevents destabilizing parameter changes while enabling systematic improvement. Our method achieves 33.9\% BLEU improvement and 36.2\% perplexity reduction on news summarization tasks while using minimal computational resources. The approach provides a practical framework for controlled model adaptation that balances performance gains with representational stability.

item.title: LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.13545v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern language models are trained on heterogeneous web-scale text corpora. Consequently, studying knowledge and skill acquisition is difficult, as prior exposure to related content is hard to characterize. To address this challenge, we introduce LittleCurriculum, a curated 88B-token pretraining corpus tailored to U.S. elementary school material, explicitly excluding concepts, facts, and vocabulary taught above Grade 5. Training a 5B-parameter LLM from scratch on LittleCurriculum yields LittleLearner, a model with sufficient language competence for open-ended evaluation, yet with clear knowledge and capability boundaries mapped to interpretable curriculum guidelines. We release LittleCurriculum and LittleLearner as a developmentally restricted sandbox to study how models acquire, represent, and use data under a well-defined training scope. We illustrate the sandbox's utility in a first suite of experiments on injecting new knowledge through post-training and in-context learning. These methods let LittleLearner better utilize existing knowledge, but do not raise out-of-scope capabilities. Our findings underscore the value of this controlled environment for future investigations.

item.title: How Language Models Organize and Structure Moral Knowledge [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.27402v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) organize moral knowledge? Models detect moral content broadly, but detection is a low bar. We ask whether they go further, distinguishing moral foundations from one another and organizing the relationships between them geometrically. We train six independent linear probes on open-weight language models, one per Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) category (care/harm, fair/cheat, lib/oppress, loy/betray, auth/subv, sanc/degrade), and examine how the resulting directions relate to each other in representation space. We find the directions neither collapse into a single moral detector nor isolate from one another. Rather, they span a near-maximal number of independent dimensions while sharing a positive common component. The shared component is the signature of integration, and it is moral-specific relative to a matched non-moral concept battery built identically (mean pairwise cosine 0.26 vs. 0.013). The geometry is consistent across architectures and scale and reaches its integration regime early in pre-training, well before probe accuracy saturates. The structure the model discovers shows no evidence of the individualizing/binding distinction predicted by Moral Foundations Theory (an underpowered test: only 10 distinct splits exist, so it cannot reject at the 0.05 level) but rather reflects corpus statistics. Extending to moral dilemmas, each dilemma direction partially composes from its component foundations, at 2.7x a mismatched-pair baseline, while the majority of its variance encodes conflict-specific structure. The model represents moral tension itself, not a pre-resolved judgment.

item.title: Attention-Mass Condensation for Sparse Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2602.06317v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Attention-mass concentration creates an opportunity for sparse decoding, but retained mass alone does not guarantee a stable greedy decision: retrieval error, omitted value directions, and recursive decoding all matter. We formalize this distinction with an exact omitted-mass identity and a sufficient downstream margin condition, then characterize a query-dependent mean-pooled block selector. On Qwen2-0.5B, a paired fresh-selection sweep covers supports of 97--769 positions, contexts of 2K--16K, and five prefixes per context. The primary exact-match result is that none of 60 runs remains identical to dense decoding through 128 tokens. Distributional quality is distinct: for supports of at least 193, seven of nine context-support conditions have median teacher-forced continuation perplexity changes within 5\% of dense, but prompt-level ranges include severe 16K outliers. All seven runs with teacher-forced match below 70\% have perplexity increases above 100\%; these observations come from two prefixes and suggest a warning regime, not a general threshold. The measured perplexity is teacher-forced on the dense model's own continuation, not the sparse model's free-running output. Separate retrieval and attention-mass probes illustrate why captured mass alone is not a retrieval or decision guarantee. Isolated operator timings do not establish matched-quality acceleration or end-to-end serving speed.

item.title: Steering Without Breaking: Mechanistically Informed Interventions for Discrete Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.10971v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising all positions in parallel, offering an alternative to autoregressive models. Controlled generation methods for DLMs, imported from autoregressive models, apply uniform intervention at every denoising step.
